summary: This informational memo argues that IETF documents tend to be written for implementers, so reviewers are overwhelmed by details. It encourages writing a protocol model that shows the essential design and makes review easier.

eli5.summary: A long instruction book is hard to check for mistakes. This document suggests writing a short model that shows how the whole thing works.

questions: how to write a protocol model
how to write a protocol model for an rfc
what three questions should a protocol model answer
subtitle: A short guide to writing the big-picture overview that lets reviewers grasp a protocol before wading into its details.

tldr.problem: IETF documents are written for implementors, so reviewers, who have little time, struggle to see the big picture of a protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends a short protocol model that answers three questions: what problem is being solved, what messages flow and what they mean, and what important but unobvious features exist. It is best shown with a few simple diagrams.
tldr.outcome: The memo defines no protocol; it is guidance, illustrated with models of STUN, DCCP, WebDAV COPY and MOVE, and IKE.

today: RFC 4101 is an Informational memo from the IAB. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it gives guidance rather than a standard.

sections.title: Why Reviewers Need a Model
sections.content:
The IETF process depends on peer review, yet many submitted documents are extremely difficult to review. Reviewers have limited time, which leads to very long review times, inadequate reviews, or both. The RFC blames the fact that most documents simply describe the protocol and leave the reviewer to work out the architecture.

That is fine for implementors, who must understand everything anyway. Reviewers instead need the big picture first, then a focus on particular points. The proposed fix is a model: a short description of the system in overview form. It can be the first section of the protocol document or a separate document, and if it is written first it can also help early design and early review.
sections.eli5: Checking a huge rulebook is slow. A short summary page helps the checker see the whole game first and then look closely at the tricky parts.

sections.title: What a Protocol Model Is For
sections.content:
A model has to answer three questions:

  • What problem is the protocol trying to achieve?
  • What messages are being transmitted and what do they mean?
  • What are the important, but unobvious, features of the protocol?

The goal is to give enough information that a reader could design a protocol roughly isomorphic to the one described, sharing its most important features. The RFC's example: choosing a KDC-based authentication model is essential to Kerberos, while using ASN.1 is a simple implementation decision. A model is explicitly not a complete or alternate description of the protocol.
sections.eli5: A good summary tells you what the game is for, what moves players make, and any sneaky rules. It does not repeat the whole rulebook.

sections.title: Three Basic Principles
sections.content:
The RFC gives three principles for presenting a model.

  • Less is more. People can hold very few pieces of information in their heads at once, so dropping detail is good.
  • Abstraction is good. Like a map versus a photograph, a model may compress several protocol elements into one abstract piece.
  • A few well-chosen details sometimes help. Describe things in the abstract, then give one concrete case to bring it into focus. Focus on the normal path, and discuss error and corner cases only when they illustrate an important point.
sections.eli5: Show a map, not a photo. Leave out the small stuff, but give one real example so people can picture it.

sections.title: Structuring a Model in Three Parts
sections.content:
The RFC recommends visual presentation: a few key diagrams with explanatory text, typically simple boxes and arrows. The model has three parts matching the three questions, each with 1 to 3 diagrams.

  • The problem. State the environments of use, the entities, and the likely scenarios. Draw the major communicating parties and, especially, the trust relationships between them, which are often unobvious.
  • A broad overview. Show the protocol messages in a ladder or boxes-and-arrows diagram, with the purpose of each message and the major data elements. This part SHOULD NOT contain detailed message descriptions; bit diagrams, ASN.1 modules and XML schema SHOULD NOT be shown. State machines are allowed but should be kept minimal.
  • Important features. An optional final part for high-level security considerations, congestion control, or an outline of an algorithm. If there are no important points to make, leave it out.

Because Internet-Drafts and RFCs must be renderable in ASCII, graphics-heavy models can be hard to produce. The RFC suggests authors may write a separate Postscript or PDF model for review, ideally with an archival version as well.
sections.eli5: Make three small pages: what we are trying to do, who says what to whom, and any tricky bits. Use boxes and arrows, and skip the tiny details.

sections.title: The Worked Examples
sections.content:
The memo demonstrates the idea with four models.

  • STUN (RFC 3489): a client behind a NAT cannot tell its external address, so a SIP session description can carry an unusable address. A STUN server tells the client the translated address, shown as a boxes-and-arrows figure with the NAT in the middle.
  • DCCP: datagram-oriented like UDP but stateful like TCP, with four phases: initiation, feature negotiation, data transfer and termination. Initiation is a three-way handshake of DCCP-Request, DCCP-Response and DCCP-Ack, with a cookie to avoid keeping server state. Feature negotiation uses Change and Confirm options, and congestion control is negotiable (CCID-2 and CCID-3).
  • WebDAV COPY and MOVE: not equivalent to COPY plus DELETE, because of quota limits, permissions that allow renaming but not creating, and creation-date properties.
  • IKE (RFC 2409): a Stage 1 handshake builds an IKE security association (Main Mode or Aggressive Mode), then Stage 2 (Quick Mode) builds AH or ESP security associations. Main Mode is six messages (3 round trips) and offers identity protection and DoS resistance; Aggressive Mode has fewer messages but neither.
sections.eli5: The memo shows four sample summaries: how to find your mailbox address behind a doorman, how to start a chat, how renaming differs from copy-then-delete, and how two strangers agree on a secret handshake.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it does not define any protocols and therefore has no security issues. The security material in the memo, such as IKE's cookie exchange and identity protection, belongs to the example models and not to the memo's own requirements.
sections.eli5: This memo is advice about writing, not a new set of rules for computers, so it adds no new safety worries.
